entities.title: Introduction to Connectionist AI (Brief)
entities.body:
# Chapter 1: Introduction to Connectionist AI (Brief)
## Contents

- [1. What Is Connectionist AI?](#1-what-is-connectionist-ai)
- [2. The Core Principles of Connectionism](#2-the-core-principles-of-connectionism)
- [3. Symbolic AI vs Connectionist AI](#3-symbolic-ai-vs-connectionist-ai)
- [4. A Short History](#4-a-short-history)
- [5. Why Did It Take So Long to Work?](#5-why-did-it-take-so-long-to-work)
- [6. Your First Neuron: A Hands-On Example](#6-your-first-neuron-a-hands-on-example)
- [7. Common Misconceptions](#7-common-misconceptions)
- [Key Takeaways](#key-takeaways)
- [Practice Questions](#practice-questions)
- [Answer Key](#answer-key)

## Key Takeaways
- Connectionism builds intelligence from many simple connected units whose weights are learned.
- It excels at messy, perceptual data; symbolic AI excels at explicit logic.
- Data, compute and better algorithms made deep learning take off around 2012.
- A single neuron is limited; layers give networks their power.

---

## Practice Questions

1. In one sentence, what is the main idea of connectionism?
2. What in an artificial network plays the role of a synapse?
3. Give one strength and one weakness of connectionist AI versus symbolic AI.
4. What is "distributed representation"?
5. Which training method was popularised for multi-layer networks in 1986?
6. Which logic function can a single neuron *not* learn?
7. Name the three ingredients behind the deep learning boom.
8. True or False: Artificial neural networks are accurate simulations of the brain.

---

## Answer Key

1. Intelligence emerges from many simple connected units whose connection strengths are learned.
2. The weight.
3. Strength: handles messy data like images. Weakness: hard to interpret (or needs lots of data).
4. A concept is spread across many units, and each unit helps represent many concepts.
5. Backpropagation.
6. XOR.
7. Data, compute (GPUs), better algorithms.
8. False. They are loose, simplified inspirations.


## 1. What Is Connectionist AI?

**Connectionism** is an approach to building intelligent systems from **many simple processing units that are linked together**. No single unit is intelligent. The behaviour of the whole system comes from **how the units are connected** and **how strong each connection is**.

![Two tiny networks receive the same inputs. Changing the weights changes how much the active input contributes and changes the score from 0.2 to 0.8.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Animated/what-is-connectionism.svg)

The idea is inspired by the brain, where billions of neurons communicate through connections called **synapses**. Learning in the brain is believed to involve strengthening or weakening these synapses. Connectionist AI copies this idea in a simplified, mathematical form:

| Biology | Artificial version |
|---|---|
| Neuron | Unit / node that computes a number |
| Synapse (connection) | **Weight**, a learnable number |
| Strengthening a synapse | Increasing a weight |
| Learning from experience | Adjusting weights to reduce error |

> **Important:** artificial neural networks are only *loosely* inspired by the brain. They are mathematical models, not accurate simulations of biology.

The most successful modern form of connectionist AI is the **artificial neural network (ANN)**, and especially **deep learning**, which uses networks with many layers.

![Four pixel inputs feed a group of hidden units. Their outputs are combined to produce two class scores.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/simple-units-together.svg)

## 2. The Core Principles of Connectionism

1. **Many simple units.** Each unit does a tiny calculation (weighted sum plus a non-linear function).
2. **Parallel processing.** Many units compute at the same time, which suits modern GPUs.
3. **Distributed representation.** A concept like "cat" is not stored in one place. It is spread across many units and weights, and one unit takes part in many concepts.
4. **Learning by adjusting weights.** Knowledge is not programmed in. It is acquired from examples.
5. **Graceful degradation.** Damaging a few units usually reduces performance slightly rather than breaking everything (unlike deleting one rule from a rule list).
6. **Generalisation.** A trained network can handle new inputs it has never seen, as long as they resemble its training data.

![A toy network represents cat and dog images with distinct patterns across five units. One unit is active in both patterns.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/distributed-patterns.svg)

![The trained model predicts the class of a handwritten digit that was held out of training.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/generalisation-example.svg)

## 3. Symbolic AI vs Connectionist AI

Early AI (1950s to 1980s) was mostly **symbolic**: experts wrote explicit rules and logic. Connectionism took a different route: learn from data.

| | Symbolic AI | Connectionist AI |
|---|---|---|
| Knowledge stored as | Explicit rules, facts, logic | Numbers (weights) in a network |
| Built by | Human experts encoding knowledge | Learning from examples |
| Handles noisy or messy input | Poorly | Well |
| Explanation of decisions | Clear | Hard |
| Needs lots of data | No | Usually yes |
| Good at | Logic, planning, exact reasoning | Perception, language, pattern recognition |
| Example | "IF temperature > 38 THEN fever" | A network trained on thousands of X-rays |

![In symbolic AI an expert supplies a rule; in connectionist AI labelled examples are used to fit weights.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/rules-and-weights.svg)

Neither approach is simply better. Modern research increasingly explores **neuro-symbolic AI**, which combines learning with explicit reasoning.

## 4. A Short History

| Year | Milestone | Why it mattered |
|---|---|---|
| 1943 | McCulloch and Pitts publish a mathematical model of a neuron | First formal "artificial neuron" |
| 1949 | Donald Hebb proposes that connections strengthen with use | Early learning principle (later paraphrased as "cells that fire together wire together") |
| 1958 | Frank Rosenblatt publishes the **Perceptron** model | Early trainable neural model |
| 1969 | Minsky and Papert show a single perceptron cannot learn XOR | Contributes to reduced interest in perceptrons; the broader **AI winter** of the 1970s had several causes |
| 1986 | Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams popularise **backpropagation** | Efficient training of multi-layer networks becomes more widely used |
| 1989 to 1998 | LeCun's convolutional networks read handwritten digits | Practical success, mostly in niche uses |
| 1997 | LSTM networks introduced | Better memory for sequences |
| 2012 | AlexNet wins the ImageNet competition by a large margin | Starts the **deep learning** boom |
| 2014 to 2016 | GANs; deep reinforcement learning beats humans at Go | Generation and decision-making breakthroughs |
| 2017 | The **Transformer** architecture is introduced | Foundation of modern language models |
| 2020s | Large-scale models for text, images, audio, code | Connectionist AI becomes mainstream |

![Four selected milestones from the perceptron to the Transformer, in chronological order.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/selected-milestones.svg)

## 5. Why Did It Take So Long to Work?

Three ingredients had to arrive together:

1. **Data.** The internet created huge datasets (photos, text, clicks, sensor data).
2. **Compute.** GPUs, originally made for video games, turned out to be ideal for the matrix maths neural networks need.
3. **Better algorithms.** Improved activation functions, optimisers, initialisation, normalisation and architectures made deep networks trainable.

![Data supplies examples, compute speeds the calculations, and training methods make updates more effective.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/training-ingredients.svg)

## 6. Your First Neuron: A Hands-On Example

A single neuron computes a **weighted sum of inputs plus a bias**, then applies a decision rule. Let's build a neuron that behaves like the logical **AND** gate (output 1 only if both inputs are 1).

Choose weights `w = [1, 1]` and bias `b = -1.5`. Rule: output 1 if the sum is greater than 0, else 0.

![An AND neuron adds the two weighted inputs and the bias to get 0.5, then outputs 1.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Animated/and-neuron.svg)

| input1 | input2 | Sum = 1·input1 + 1·input2 − 1.5 | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0 | −1.5 | 0 |
| 1 | 0 | −0.5 | 0 |
| 0 | 1 | −0.5 | 0 |
| 1 | 1 | 0.5 | 1 |

It works. Here we chose the weights by hand. A *learning* algorithm would find them automatically from examples, which is the whole point of connectionism.

```python
def neuron(input1, input2, w=(1, 1), bias=-1.5):
    value = w[0]*input1 + w[1]*input2 + bias
    return 1 if value > 0 else 0

for input1 in (0, 1):
    for input2 in (0, 1):
        print(input1, input2, "->", neuron(input1, input2))
```

![The AND boundary separates the single positive example from the three negative examples.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/and-input-space.svg)

**The XOR problem.** XOR (output 1 if the inputs *differ*) cannot be solved by any single neuron, because no straight line separates its 1s from its 0s. Adding a **hidden layer** solves it. This is exactly why multi-layer networks matter (Chapter 2).

![The XOR 0s and 1s occupy opposite corners of a square, so a straight line cannot separate the two groups.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/xor-boundary.svg)

![Two hidden detectors answer whether at least one input is active and whether both are active. Together they distinguish exactly one active input.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/xor-hidden-layer.svg)

## 7. Common Misconceptions

- **"Neural networks work like the brain."** They are loosely inspired by it and far simpler.
- **"More layers is always better."** Deeper networks need more data and care, and can overfit.
- **"It's a black box nobody understands."** Much is understood about training and behaviour, but explaining individual decisions is hard, and active research (interpretability) addresses it.
- **"AI means neural networks."** AI also includes symbolic methods, search, probabilistic models and more.

![During training, targets help update the weights. During prediction, the weights stay fixed.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/train-vs-use.svg)

entities.summary: Chapter 2 · Basic Concepts, Terminology and Architectures of Neural Networks
entities.body:
# Chapter 2: Basic Concepts, Terminology and Architectures of Neural Networks
## Contents

- [1. The Artificial Neuron](#1-the-artificial-neuron)
- [2. Essential Terminology](#2-essential-terminology)
- [3. Layers and Matrix Form](#3-layers-and-matrix-form)
- [4. A Complete Worked Example: Forward Pass, Loss and One Weight Update](#4-a-complete-worked-example-forward-pass-loss-and-one-weight-update)
- [5. What Backpropagation Really Is](#5-what-backpropagation-really-is)
- [6. The Learning Loop](#6-the-learning-loop)
- [7. Common Loss Functions](#7-common-loss-functions)
- [8. Architectures](#8-architectures)
- [9. How to Choose an Architecture](#9-how-to-choose-an-architecture)
- [10. Tiny Code Example (PyTorch)](#10-tiny-code-example-pytorch)
- [11. Common Beginner Mistakes](#11-common-beginner-mistakes)
- [Key Takeaways](#key-takeaways)
- [Practice Questions](#practice-questions)
- [Answer Key](#answer-key)

## Key Takeaways
- A neuron = weighted sum + bias + activation.
- A network is layers of neurons; parameters = weights + biases.
- Training = forward pass, loss, backpropagation, update, repeated.
- Choose the architecture to match the data's structure.

---

## Practice Questions

1. Compute a ReLU neuron with inputs `[2, 1]`, weights `[0.4, 0.6]`, bias `-1`.
2. Parameters in a dense layer with 5 inputs and 3 neurons?
3. 2,000 samples, batch size 250: how many iterations per epoch?
4. Order these: update weights, forward pass, compute loss, backward pass.
5. Which neural network architecture suits (a) photos, (b) spreadsheet, (c) translation?
6. What problem do LSTM gates help solve?
7. What does validation loss rising while training loss falls indicate?
8. Why is a bias term useful?

---

## Answer Key

1. z = 0.8 + 0.6 − 1 = 0.4, ReLU → **0.4**.
2. 5×3 + 3 = **18**.
3. 2000 / 250 = **8**.
4. Forward pass → loss → backward pass → update.
5. (a) CNN, (b) MLP, (c) Transformer. For plain spreadsheet data, try gradient boosting or a linear model as a baseline first.
6. Vanishing gradients and forgetting over long sequences.
7. Overfitting.
8. It shifts the activation threshold so the neuron isn't forced through the origin.



## 1. The Artificial Neuron

### 1.1 How Does an Artificial Neuron Work?

A neuron performs three simple steps:

1. **Multiply:** Multiply each input by its weight.
2. **Add:** Add all the results together, then add the bias.
3. **Activate:** Apply an activation function to get the final output.

```text
z = (w1 × x1) + (w2 × x2) + ... + b
output = activation(z)
```

- `x`: Input values.
- `w`: Weights that determine the importance of each input.
- `b`: Bias, which adjusts the neuron's calculation.
- `z`: Result before applying the activation function.

![Two equal inputs contribute different amounts because of their weights. The negative contribution leaves the sum below zero even after adding the bias, so ReLU outputs zero.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/weighted-neuron.svg)

**Why do we need bias?**

Bias allows a neuron to adjust its activation threshold. Without bias, the neuron's decision boundary must pass through the origin. Think of it as the `b` in the equation `y = mx + b`.

![With weight 1, changing the bias from 0 to −2 moves the input threshold from 0 to 2.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/bias-threshold.svg)

**Worked Example**

Suppose we have:
- Inputs: `x = [1, 2]`
- Weights: `w = [0.5, -0.3]`
- Bias: `b = 0.4`

First, multiply the inputs by their weights and add the bias:

```text
z = (0.5 × 1) + (-0.3 × 2) + 0.4
z = 0.5 - 0.6 + 0.4
z = 0.3
```

Now, apply an activation function:

**ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit):** Converts negative values to 0 while keeping positive values unchanged. Formula: `max(0, z)`.
- **ReLU:** `max(0, 0.3)` = **0.3**

**Sigmoid:** Converts any input into a value between 0 and 1. Often used when the output represents a probability.
- **Sigmoid:** `1 / (1 + e^-0.3)` ≈ **0.574**

Both functions receive the same value but produce different outputs.

**Understanding Weights:**

- Positive weight: Increases the neuron's result.
- Negative weight: Decreases the neuron's result.
- Larger absolute weight: Has a stronger influence on the result.

## 2. Essential Terminology

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Feature** | One input variable (a pixel, a price, a word embedding value) |
| **Input layer** | Receives the raw features. It does no computation |
| **Hidden layer** | Layers between input and output that learn intermediate features |
| **Output layer** | Produces the final prediction |
| **Weight** | Learned strength of a connection |
| **Bias** | Learned offset added before the activation |
| **Activation function** | Non-linear function applied to a neuron's sum (Chapter 4) |
| **Parameters** | All learnable numbers (weights and biases) |
| **Hyperparameters** | Settings chosen by *you*: learning rate, layers, units, batch size |
| **Forward pass** | Computing the output from the input |
| **Loss / cost function** | A number measuring how wrong the prediction is |
| **Backpropagation** | Computes how much each weight contributed to the loss |
| **Gradient** | The slope of the loss with respect to a parameter |
| **Gradient descent** | Moves parameters in the direction that reduces loss |
| **Learning rate** | Size of each update step |
| **Epoch** | One full pass through the training data |
| **Batch / mini-batch** | A subset of the data used for one update |
| **Iteration** | One update step (one batch) |
| **Overfitting** | Memorising training data, performing poorly on new data |
| **Underfitting** | Too simple to capture the pattern |
| **Generalisation** | Performing well on unseen data |
| **Training / validation / test sets** | Fit the weights / tune choices / final honest check |
| **Depth** | Number of layers. **Width** is the units per layer |

**Epochs, batches and iterations.** If you have 1,000 samples and a batch size of 100, one epoch = 10 iterations.

![One thousand training examples form ten batches of one hundred. With one update per batch, a full epoch contains ten updates.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/batches-and-epochs.svg)

## 3. Layers and Matrix Form

A **dense (fully connected) layer** is a group of neurons where every neuron receives input from every neuron in the previous layer. Each connection has its own weight, and each neuron has its own bias.

For an entire layer, we can calculate all neuron outputs at once using:

```text
h = activation(W · x + b)
```

- `x`: Input vector containing the values passed into the layer (size `n_in`).
- `W`: Weight matrix containing the weights of all connections (size `n_out × n_in`).
- `b`: Bias vector, with one bias for each neuron (size `n_out`).
- `activation`: An activation function such as ReLU or Sigmoid.
- `h`: The output vector produced by the layer.

**How it works:** The layer multiplies each input by its corresponding weight, adds the biases, and applies an activation function to produce its outputs.

![A dense layer with three inputs and two neurons has one row of three weights and one bias for each output.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/matrix-layer.svg)

**Parameter count of a dense layer** = `(n_in × n_out) + n_out`.

Parameters are the values (weights and biases) that a neural network learns during training.

**Example: 3 inputs → 4 neurons**
- Weights: 3 × 4 = 12
- Biases: 4 (one for each neuron)
- Total: 12 + 4 = **16 parameters**.

A network `3 → 4 → 4 → 1` has three sets of connections (one between each pair of neighbouring layers):

- Layer 1: (3 × 4 + 4) = 16
- Layer 2: (4 × 4 + 4) = 20
- Layer 3: (4 × 1 + 1) = 5

Total: 16 + 20 + 5 = **41 trainable parameters**.

## 4. A Complete Worked Example: Forward Pass, Loss and One Weight Update

A neural network learns by making predictions, checking how far they are from the correct answers, and adjusting its weights to reduce errors.

This process has four main steps:

1. **Forward Pass:** Calculate the network's prediction using the given inputs, weights, and biases.
2. **Loss Calculation:** Measure how far the prediction is from the correct answer.
3. **Backward Pass (Backpropagation):** Calculate how much a weight contributes to the error using derivatives and the chain rule.
4. **Weight Update:** Adjust the weight to reduce the error.

**Network Structure:**

A network with 2 inputs → 2 hidden neurons (ReLU) → 1 output neuron (linear).

Input: `x = [1, 2]`

Correct answer (target): `y = 1`

Hidden layer:
- Neuron 1: weights `[0.5, -0.3]`, bias `0.4`
- Neuron 2: weights `[0.2, 0.4]`, bias `-0.1`

Output neuron: weights `[1.0, -0.5]`, bias `0.2`.

![Signals travel from both inputs to both ReLU neurons, then combine at the output to predict 0.05.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Animated/worked-network.svg)

### 4.1 Step 1: Forward Pass (Making a Prediction)

First, calculate the outputs of both hidden neurons using their weights, biases, and ReLU activation function.

```text
h1 = ReLU(0.5 × 1 + (-0.3) × 2 + 0.4)
h1 = ReLU(0.3) = 0.3

h2 = ReLU(0.2 × 1 + 0.4 × 2 - 0.1)
h2 = ReLU(0.9) = 0.9
```

Next, use these two outputs as inputs for the output neuron. Since it uses a linear activation, we simply calculate the weighted sum and add the bias.

```text
ŷ = 1.0 × 0.3 + (-0.5) × 0.9 + 0.2
ŷ = 0.3 - 0.45 + 0.2
ŷ = 0.05
```

The network's prediction is **0.05**, while the correct answer is **1**.

### 4.2 Step 2: Loss Calculation (Measuring the Error)

Loss measures how far the network's prediction is from the correct answer. Here, we use **Squared Error**, which squares the difference between the prediction and the target.

Formula:

```text
L = (Prediction - Target)²
```

Calculation:

```text
L = (ŷ - y)²
L = (0.05 - 1)²
L = (-0.95)²
L = 0.9025
```

The loss is **0.9025**. A smaller loss means the prediction is closer to the correct answer.

### 4.3 Step 3: Backward Pass (Calculating the Error's Effect)

Backpropagation calculates how much each weight affects the loss. This information helps the network decide how to adjust its weights.

For this example, we will only calculate the gradient for the output weight `v1 = 1.0` (from hidden neuron 1 to the output).

Using the **chain rule**, we calculate:

```text
dL/dŷ = 2(ŷ - y)
      = 2(0.05 - 1)
      = -1.9

dŷ/dv1 = h1
       = 0.3

dL/dv1 = (-1.9) × 0.3
       = -0.57
```

The result `-0.57` is the gradient. It tells us how changing this weight affects the loss.

Note: This example only calculates the gradient for one weight. A complete training process calculates gradients for all trainable weights and biases.

### 4.4 Step 4: Weight Update (Learning from the Error)

Now, we adjust the weight using the gradient and a value called the **learning rate**.

The learning rate controls how big each weight adjustment is. Here, we use `0.1`.

Formula:

```text
New Weight = Old Weight - (Learning Rate × Gradient)
```

Calculation:

```text
v1_new = 1.0 - (0.1 × -0.57)
v1_new = 1.0 + 0.057
v1_new = 1.057
```

The new weight is **1.057**, increased from 1.0.

This adjustment moves the prediction closer to the target value of 1.

### 4.5 What Happens Next?

![One training step predicts 0.05, computes a loss of 0.9025 and a gradient of −0.57, then updates the output weight to 1.057.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Animated/training-step.svg)

The network repeats these steps during training:

- Make predictions using a forward pass.
- Calculate the loss to measure errors.
- Use backpropagation to calculate gradients.
- Update weights and biases using the gradients.

Repeating this process across many batches (groups of training examples) and epochs (complete passes through the training dataset) allows the network to gradually improve its predictions.
## 5. What Backpropagation Really Is

Backpropagation uses the **chain rule of calculus** to calculate how much each weight affects the loss. It works backward from the output, reusing calculations to efficiently find gradients for all weights. Its computational cost is typically a small multiple of a forward pass.

Libraries like PyTorch and TensorFlow automate this using **automatic differentiation**:

```python
import torch

v1 = torch.tensor(1.0, requires_grad=True)
h1 = torch.tensor(0.3)
h2 = torch.tensor(0.9)

loss = (v1 * h1 + (-0.5) * h2 + 0.2 - 1.0) ** 2
loss.backward()

print(v1.grad)  # tensor(-0.5700)
```

`loss.backward()` automatically calculates the gradient of the loss with respect to `v1`.

![The forward pass moves from weight to prediction to loss. The backward pass follows the same dependencies in reverse and multiplies local derivatives.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Animated/chain-rule-path.svg)

## 6. The Learning Loop

1. **Forward pass:** make a prediction
2. **Compute loss:** compare with the truth
3. **Backward pass:** compute gradients
4. **Update:** `w ← w − learning_rate × gradient`
5. Repeat over batches and epochs, monitoring validation loss

![On a toy squared loss surface, successive gradient descent steps move closer to zero.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Animated/descent-steps.svg)

## 7. Common Loss Functions

| Task | Output layer | Loss |
|---|---|---|
| Regression | Linear | Mean Squared Error (MSE) or MAE |
| Binary classification | Sigmoid | Binary cross-entropy |
| Multi-class classification | Softmax | Categorical cross-entropy |

**Cross-entropy example.** If the true class gets predicted probability 0.7, the loss is −ln(0.7) ≈ **0.357**. Probability 0.99 gives 0.010; probability 0.1 gives 2.30. Confident wrong answers are punished heavily.

![As errors grow, absolute error rises in a straight line and squared error rises increasingly quickly.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/loss-shapes.svg)

## 8. Architectures

### 8.1 Feedforward Network / Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP)
- Information flows one way, input → hidden → output.
- Every layer is dense.
- **Use for:** tabular data, simple regression and classification, and as building blocks inside bigger models.
- **Limit:** ignores structure (it doesn't know pixels are neighbours or that words come in order).

### 8.2 Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)
- A small **filter (kernel)** slides over the image, detecting a local pattern wherever it appears.
- **Weight sharing:** the same filter is reused across positions, so far fewer parameters than a dense layer.
- **Pooling** reduces size and adds tolerance to small shifts.
- Early layers detect edges, later layers detect textures, parts and objects.

![A two-by-two edge filter scans nine patches of an image. Each patch contributes one score at the corresponding location in the feature map.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Animated/cnn-filter-scan.svg)

**Useful formulas**
- Output size = `floor((n − k + 2p) / s) + 1` (input size n, kernel k, padding p, stride s; dilation 1). `floor` means round down.
  Example: n = 32, k = 3, p = 1, s = 1 → (32 − 3 + 2)/1 + 1 = **32**.
- Parameters of a conv layer = `(k × k × c_in + 1) × c_out`.
  Example: 3×3 kernel, 3 input channels, 16 filters → (27 + 1) × 16 = **448**.

**Use for:** images, video, audio spectrograms, also some text and time series (1D convolution).

![Each coloured 2 by 2 block becomes one number, its largest value, in the pooled output.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/max-pooling.svg)

### 8.3 Recurrent Networks: RNN, LSTM, GRU

![Three copies of the same recurrent cell show how the hidden state passes from one sequence step to the next.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Animated/rnn-state.svg)

A basic RNN keeps a **hidden state** that carries information through a sequence:

```
h_t = tanh(Wx · x_t + Wh · h_(t-1) + b)
```
- **Problem:** gradients vanish over long sequences, so it forgets distant history.
- **LSTM** adds a **cell state** and three **gates** (forget, input, output) that decide what to erase, store and reveal.
- **GRU** is a lighter two-gate version.
- **Use for:** time series, speech, older text models. Largely replaced by Transformers in language, but still useful for small sequence tasks.

![An LSTM filters the old memory and new candidate before adding them. The output gate controls the exposed state.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/lstm-gates.svg)

### 8.4 Transformer
- Uses **self-attention**: each element of a sequence computes how relevant every other element is, then mixes information accordingly.

![In an example attention head, the updated representation of “it” mixes information from three tokens with different weights.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/attention-mix.svg)

```
Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q·Kᵀ / √d) · V
```
- Processes the whole sequence **in parallel** (fast on GPUs) and captures long-range relationships directly.
- Needs **positional encodings**, since it has no built-in notion of order.
- **Use for:** language, and increasingly vision, audio, time series and multimodal tasks.

### 8.5 Autoencoder
- **Encoder** compresses input into a small **latent code**; **decoder** reconstructs the input from it.
- Trained to minimise reconstruction error, with no labels needed.
- **Use for:** dimensionality reduction, denoising, **anomaly detection** (anomalies reconstruct poorly).
- **Variational autoencoders (VAEs)** learn a smooth latent space that can generate new samples.

![An encoder compresses the input into a small code. The decoder reconstructs the input, and training compares the reconstruction with the original.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/autoencoder-bottleneck.svg)

### 8.6 Generative Adversarial Network (GAN)
- **Generator** creates fake samples; **discriminator** tries to tell real from fake. They improve by competing.
- **Use for:** realistic image synthesis. Training can be unstable.

![A discriminator sees both training examples and generated examples. Its feedback trains the generator.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/gan-feedback.svg)

### 8.7 Other Types Worth Knowing
- **Graph neural networks (GNNs):** data shaped as nodes and edges (molecules, social networks).
- **Diffusion models:** generate images by learning to remove noise step by step.

![Three neighbors send messages to a central graph node, which combines them with its own features.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/graph-messages.svg)

### 8.8 Architecture Comparison

| Architecture | Typical data | Key idea | Main strength | Main limitation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MLP | Tabular | Dense layers | Simple, flexible | Ignores structure |
| CNN | Images | Local filters, shared weights | Efficient for spatial data | Limited long-range context |
| RNN/LSTM | Sequences | Hidden state | Handles variable length | Slow, hard to parallelise |
| Transformer | Text, sequences | Attention | Long-range, parallel | Memory heavy for long inputs |
| Autoencoder | Any | Compress and reconstruct | Unsupervised features | Reconstruction ≠ usefulness |
| GAN | Images | Generator vs discriminator | Sharp samples | Unstable training |

## 9. How to Choose an Architecture

1. Look at your **data type** (table, image, sequence, graph).
2. Start with the **simplest sensible model** (try gradient boosting or a linear model for plain tabular data; an MLP is a neural option, and pre-trained models suit many image and text tasks).
3. Build a **baseline** first, then add complexity only if needed.
4. Prefer **transfer learning** (reuse a pre-trained network) when data is limited.

## 10. Tiny Code Example (PyTorch)

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(2, 2),   # input 2 -> hidden 2
    nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(2, 1)    # hidden 2 -> output 1
)

x = torch.tensor([[1.0, 2.0]])
y = torch.tensor([[1.0]])

loss_fn = nn.MSELoss()
opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.1)

for step in range(100):
    opt.zero_grad()
    loss = loss_fn(model(x), y)
    loss.backward()
    opt.step()

print(model(x).item())   # close to 1.0
```

## 11. Common Beginner Mistakes
- Forgetting to **scale inputs**, which makes training slow or unstable.
- Evaluating on training data only.
- Using softmax **and** a loss that already includes softmax (e.g. PyTorch `CrossEntropyLoss` expects raw scores).
- Making the network far bigger than the data justifies.


## Reading note

A positive weight raises the preactivation when its input increases, holding other inputs fixed. The sign of the contribution w × x also depends on the input's sign.

entities.title: Applications of Neural Networks (Brief)
entities.body:
# Chapter 3: Applications of Neural Networks (Brief)
## Contents

- [1. Why So Many Applications?](#1-why-so-many-applications)
- [2. Major Application Areas](#2-major-application-areas)
- [3. Quick Reference](#3-quick-reference)
- [4. A Typical Project Pipeline](#4-a-typical-project-pipeline)
- [5. When Is a Neural Network a Good Fit?](#5-when-is-a-neural-network-a-good-fit)
- [6. Mini Case Study: Defect Detection on a Production Line](#6-mini-case-study-defect-detection-on-a-production-line)
- [7. Responsible Use](#7-responsible-use)
- [Key Takeaways](#key-takeaways)
- [Practice Questions](#practice-questions)
- [Answer Key](#answer-key)

## Key Takeaways
- The same core idea adapts to many tasks by choosing the right architecture.
- Match the **metric** to the real-world cost of errors.
- Start with a baseline; deploy with monitoring.
- Neural networks are powerful but not always the best tool.

---

## Practice Questions

1. Match task to model: (a) defect photos, (b) translation, (c) unusual machine behaviour, no fault labels.
2. Name two situations where a neural network is a poor choice.
3. Why track recall, not just accuracy, in fraud detection?
4. Why monitor a model after deployment?
5. What baseline would you try first on a plain spreadsheet dataset?
6. Name one risk of using biased training data.

---

## Answer Key

1. (a) CNN, (b) Transformer, (c) Autoencoder.
2. E.g. tiny datasets; a simple rule already works; full explainability required.
3. Fraud is rare, so a model can be highly "accurate" while missing most fraud.
4. Real-world data changes, so performance can silently degrade.
5. Gradient boosting or a linear model.
6. The model learns and repeats unfair patterns, harming some groups.


## 1. Why So Many Applications?

Neural networks are **universal function approximators**: with suitable activations and enough units, they can approximate any continuous function on a closed, bounded input domain to any desired accuracy. This does not guarantee that training will find the right weights or that the model will generalise well. Different architectures (Chapter 2) specialise the idea for images, sequences, graphs and more. This is why the same toolbox spans medicine, finance, entertainment and engineering.

Most applications fall into a few **task types**:

| Task type | Output | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Classification** | A category | Spam or not spam |
| **Regression** | A number | Predicted house price |
| **Detection / segmentation** | Where things are | Locating pedestrians in an image |
| **Sequence prediction** | Next items or a translation | Forecasting, speech-to-text |
| **Generation** | New content | Text, images, music |
| **Decision-making (RL)** | Actions | Robot control, game play |
| **Ranking / retrieval** | Ordered list | Search results, recommendations |
| **Anomaly detection** | Normal vs unusual | Machine failure alerts |

## 2. Major Application Areas

### 2.1 Computer Vision
- **Tasks:** image classification, object detection, segmentation, face recognition, OCR.
- **Models:** CNNs, Vision Transformers.
- **Examples:** phone face unlock, factory defect inspection, crop disease detection, self-driving perception.
- **Metrics:** accuracy, precision/recall, mean average precision (mAP).
- **Watch out for:** lighting and camera changes between training and real use.

![Classification labels a whole image, detection draws boxes around objects, and segmentation labels their pixels.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/vision-outputs.svg)

### 2.2 Natural Language Processing (NLP)
- **Tasks:** translation, summarisation, question answering, sentiment analysis, chatbots, search.
- **Models:** Transformers (including large language models).
- **Metrics:** accuracy/F1 for classification, BLEU or human ratings for generation.
- **Watch out for:** factual mistakes, bias in text data, privacy of user text.

![A text model maps the tokens in a sentence to one sentiment label.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/text-token-label.svg)

### 2.3 Speech and Audio
- **Tasks:** speech recognition, voice assistants, speaker identification, music tagging.
- **Models:** CNNs on spectrograms, RNNs, Transformers.
- **Metric:** word error rate (WER).

![Speech recognition turns a waveform into audio features and decodes a sequence of text tokens.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/speech-to-text.svg)

### 2.4 Forecasting and Time Series
- **Tasks:** demand, energy load, traffic, weather, finance.
- **Models:** MLPs, LSTMs, temporal convolution, Transformers.
- **Metrics:** MAE, RMSE, quantile loss.

![Observed values end at a cutoff. Future predictions begin at that cutoff with a widening uncertainty band.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/forecast-window.svg)

### 2.5 Recommendation
- **Tasks:** suggest products, videos, music, news.
- **Models:** embeddings plus MLPs, two-tower models, sequence models.

![Sorting three candidates by score puts item B first, then C, then A.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/ranking-scores.svg)

### 2.6 Healthcare and Life Sciences
- **Tasks:** detecting disease in X-rays, CT and pathology images; predicting patient risk; protein structure prediction; drug discovery.
- **Models:** CNNs, Transformers, graph networks.
- **Watch out for:** small labelled datasets, strict regulation, need for explanation and human oversight.

![A model flags an image region for a clinician to review alongside other evidence.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/clinical-review.svg)

### 2.7 Finance
- **Tasks:** fraud detection, credit scoring, risk modelling, algorithmic trading signals.
- **Models:** MLPs, autoencoders, sequence models.
- **Watch out for:** rare events (fraud is a tiny fraction of transactions), changing behaviour (concept drift), fairness and regulation.

![Example transaction risk scores above a review threshold are routed for further review.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/fraud-threshold.svg)

### 2.8 Robotics, Control and Games
- **Tasks:** walking robots, warehouse picking, game agents, chip design, data-centre cooling.
- **Models:** deep reinforcement learning combined with vision networks.

![A game agent sends an action to the environment, which returns the next observation and a reward.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Animated/rl-feedback.svg)

### 2.9 Generative AI
- **Tasks:** text, image, audio, video and code generation.
- **Models:** Transformers, diffusion models, GANs, VAEs.

![The model predicts a token, appends it to the prefix, and uses the extended prefix for the next prediction.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Animated/next-token-generation.svg)

### 2.10 Anomaly Detection and Monitoring
- **Tasks:** machine failure prediction, network intrusion, medical monitoring.
- **Models:** autoencoders trained on normal data; anything reconstructed poorly is flagged.

![On a reconstruction-error scale, examples to the right of a chosen threshold are flagged for review.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/anomaly-threshold.svg)

## 3. Quick Reference

| Area | Typical input | Typical model | Key metric |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vision | Images | CNN / ViT | Accuracy, mAP |
| Language | Text | Transformer | F1, BLEU |
| Speech | Audio | CNN / Transformer | WER |
| Forecasting | Time series | LSTM / Transformer | MAE, quantile loss |
| Recommendation | Interactions | Embeddings + MLP | Precision@K, NDCG |
| Fraud | Transactions | MLP / autoencoder | Recall, precision |
| Control | State | Deep RL | Cumulative reward |

## 4. A Typical Project Pipeline

1. **Define the problem and success metric** (including the business cost of errors).
2. **Collect and label data.** Often the hardest and most expensive step.
3. **Clean and split data** into train, validation and test sets.
4. **Build a simple baseline** (a rule, a linear model). Know what you need to beat.
5. **Train and tune** a neural network.
6. **Evaluate honestly** on unseen data, including edge cases.
7. **Deploy** (as an API, on a phone, on a device).
8. **Monitor and update**: performance degrades as the world changes.

![Use training data to fit weights, validation data to choose settings, and held-out test data to evaluate the selected model.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/dataset-split.svg)

## 5. When Is a Neural Network a Good Fit?

**Good fit**
- Large amounts of data
- Unstructured inputs (images, audio, text) or complex non-linear patterns
- Accuracy matters more than a simple explanation
- You can use a **pre-trained model** and fine-tune it

**Poor fit**
- Very small datasets (gradient boosting or linear models often win)
- A simple known rule or formula already solves the problem
- Strict requirement to explain every decision
- Very limited compute or latency budget (though small networks can still work)

> **Rule of thumb:** for plain tabular data, try gradient boosting (e.g. XGBoost, LightGBM) as a baseline. It frequently matches or beats neural networks.

![A simple rule gets 82 correct and a neural model gets 85 correct on the same illustrative test set of 100 examples.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/baseline-compare.svg)

## 6. Mini Case Study: Defect Detection on a Production Line

- **Problem:** catch faulty bottles automatically.
- **Data:** 20,000 photos, labelled "ok" or "defect" (only 2% defective).
- **Model:** a pre-trained CNN fine-tuned on the photos.
- **Challenge:** class imbalance. Accuracy of 98% is achievable by always saying "ok", so track **recall on defects** and **precision**, and use class weights or oversampling.
- **Deployment:** camera feeds images to the model; uncertain cases go to a human inspector.
- **Monitoring:** if lighting or bottle design changes, retrain.

![A camera photographs each bottle, a CNN scores the image, and uncertain cases go to a human inspector.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Animated/defect-detection.svg)

![Out of 100 representative bottles, always predicting OK gets 98 correct but catches neither of the two defects.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/accuracy-trap.svg)

![Bright and dim photos of the same bottle show how deployment images can differ from training images.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/lighting-shift.svg)

## 7. Responsible Use
- **Bias:** models copy biases in training data. Check performance across groups.
- **Privacy:** minimise and protect personal data.
- **Reliability and safety:** test realistic and rare cases; keep a **human in the loop** for high-stakes decisions.
- **Transparency:** document what the model is for, its data, and its limits.

![The same model scores 90 percent overall, 98 percent on one group, and 82 percent on an equally sized group.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/subgroup-evaluation.svg)

entities.body:
# Chapter 4: Deep Learning and Activation Functions
## Contents

- [1. What Is Deep Learning?](#1-what-is-deep-learning)
- [2. Why We Need Activation Functions](#2-why-we-need-activation-functions)
- [3. The Activation Functions](#3-the-activation-functions)
- [4. How to Choose](#4-how-to-choose)
- [5. Gradients Through Activations](#5-gradients-through-activations)
- [6. Weight Initialisation](#6-weight-initialisation)
- [7. Code](#7-code)
- [8. Common Mistakes](#8-common-mistakes)
- [Key Takeaways](#key-takeaways)
- [Practice Questions](#practice-questions)
- [Answer Key](#answer-key)

## Key Takeaways
- Depth lets networks build features in stages; activations make that useful.
- Without non-linear activations, any network collapses to a linear model.
- **ReLU** for hidden layers, **sigmoid/softmax/linear** for outputs, depending on the task.
- Vanishing gradients come from repeated multiplication by small derivatives; ReLU, good initialisation, normalisation and skip connections can reduce it.

---

## Practice Questions

1. Why can't stacked linear layers learn curved boundaries?
2. Compute ReLU(−2), ReLU(3.5), sigmoid(0).
3. Output activation for (a) spam/not spam, (b) digits 0–9, (c) house price?
4. Softmax of `[1, 1, 1]`?
5. What is the maximum slope of sigmoid?
6. What is "dying ReLU" and one fix?
7. Name two ways to reduce vanishing gradients.
8. Which activation suits an output that must be strictly positive?
9. Which initialisation pairs with ReLU?

---

## Answer Key

1. They collapse into a single linear function.
2. 0, 3.5, 0.5.
3. (a) Sigmoid, (b) Softmax, (c) Linear.
4. Each 1/3 ≈ 0.333.
5. 0.25.
6. A neuron stuck outputting 0 has zero gradient and stops learning. Fix: Leaky ReLU.
7. E.g. ReLU activations, residual connections, batch/layer normalisation, He initialisation.
8. Softplus. ReLU can output zero, so it does not guarantee a strictly positive output.
9. He initialisation.


## 1. What Is Deep Learning?

**Deep learning** is machine learning with neural networks that have **many hidden layers**. Each layer transforms its input into a slightly more abstract representation:

```
Image: pixels → edges → textures → object parts → whole objects
Text:  characters → words → phrases → sentence meaning
Audio: waveform → sounds → phonemes → words
```

This is called **hierarchical feature learning**. Before deep learning, engineers designed features by hand (e.g. edge detectors). Deep networks **learn the features automatically** from raw data.

![An illustrative image network combines pixels into edges, edges into a part, and parts into a wheel-like pattern.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/feature-hierarchy.svg)

### 1.1 Why Depth?
- **Efficiency:** some functions need exponentially many units in a single wide layer but far fewer in a deep one.
- **Reuse:** early layers learn general features reused by later layers.
- **Universal approximation:** with suitable activations and enough neurons, even a single hidden layer can approximate any continuous function on a closed, bounded input domain to any desired accuracy. Deep networks can represent some functions with far fewer parameters, but better generalisation is not guaranteed.

### 1.2 Depth vs Width
| | Deeper | Wider |
|---|---|---|
| Learns | Hierarchies of features | More features per level |
| Risk | Harder to train (vanishing gradients) | Many parameters, can overfit |
| Fix | Residual connections, normalisation | Regularisation |

![One hidden layer with five units illustrates width, while three hidden layers with three units each illustrate depth.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/depth-and-width.svg)

## 2. Why We Need Activation Functions

Without an activation, every layer is linear: `y = W·x + b`. Stacking two linear layers:

```
y1 = W1·x + b1
y2 = W2·y1 + b2 = W2·(W1·x + b1) + b2 = (W2·W1)·x + (W2·b1 + b2)
```

That is just **one** linear layer with a new weight matrix. No matter how many linear layers you stack, the result is still a straight-line (linear) function. It can never learn XOR, curved boundaries, or anything non-linear.

An **activation function** is a non-linear function applied after each layer's sum. It is what allows depth to add power.

**Desirable properties of an activation**
- **Non-linear**
- **Differentiable** (almost everywhere), so gradients can flow
- **Cheap to compute**
- **Well-behaved gradients** (not too small or too large)

![A composition of affine layers still graphs as a straight line. Adding ReLU can create a bend.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/affine-composition.svg)

## 3. The Activation Functions

![Plots of sigmoid, tanh, ReLU, and leaky ReLU. ReLU stays flat for negative inputs, while leaky ReLU keeps a small positive slope.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/activation-curves.svg)

### 3.1 Reference Values

| z | sigmoid(z) | tanh(z) | ReLU(z) | Leaky ReLU (0.01) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| −2 | 0.119 | −0.964 | 0 | −0.02 |
| −1 | 0.269 | −0.762 | 0 | −0.01 |
| 0 | 0.500 | 0.000 | 0 | 0 |
| 1 | 0.731 | 0.762 | 1 | 1 |
| 2 | 0.881 | 0.964 | 2 | 2 |

### 3.2 Sigmoid (Logistic)
```
σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e^-z)          range (0, 1)
σ'(z) = σ(z) · (1 − σ(z))      max slope = 0.25 (at z = 0)
```
- **Pros:** smooth; output interpretable as a probability.
- **Cons:** **saturates** (slope near 0 when |z| is large); outputs not zero-centred; exponential is costly.
- **Use today:** output layer of **binary classification**, and gates in LSTMs. Rarely in hidden layers.

![The sigmoid is steepest near zero and almost flat at either extreme.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/sigmoid-saturation.svg)

### 3.3 Tanh
```
tanh(z) = (e^z − e^-z) / (e^z + e^-z)     range (−1, 1)
tanh'(z) = 1 − tanh²(z)                   max slope = 1
```
- **Pros:** zero-centred; stronger gradients than sigmoid.
- **Cons:** still saturates at the extremes.
- **Use:** LSTM/GRU internals, some small networks, outputs that must be in (−1, 1).

![Tanh maps zero to zero and maps equal-magnitude inputs to outputs of equal magnitude and opposite signs.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/tanh-zero-centred.svg)

### 3.4 ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit)
```
ReLU(z) = max(0, z)
ReLU'(z) = 1 if z > 0, else 0
```
- **Pros:** very cheap; no saturation for positive z, so gradients flow well; produces **sparse** activations (many zeros); trains fast.
- **Cons:** **dying ReLU.** If a neuron's input is always negative, its output and gradient are both 0 forever, so it never recovers. Not zero-centred.
- **Use:** the **default hidden-layer activation** for MLPs and CNNs.

### 3.5 Leaky ReLU and PReLU
```
LeakyReLU(z) = z        if z > 0
               α·z      otherwise     (α = 0.01 typical)
```
- Keeps a small gradient for negative inputs, avoiding dead neurons.
- **PReLU** makes α a learned parameter.

![A magnified view shows the small negative-input slope of leaky ReLU compared with the flat ReLU.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/relu-negative-zoom.svg)

### 3.6 ELU and SELU
- **ELU:** `z` if z > 0, else `α(e^z − 1)`. Smooth, pushes mean activations toward zero.
- **SELU:** a scaled ELU that can make networks self-normalise (needs specific initialisation).

![ELU and SELU have different negative limits and different slopes on the positive side.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/elu-selu.svg)

### 3.7 GELU and Swish (SiLU)
```
GELU(z) = z · Φ(z)        (Φ = standard normal CDF)
Swish(z) = z · σ(z)
```
- Smooth, non-monotonic cousins of ReLU that often train slightly better.
- **GELU** is standard in **Transformers**; **Swish/SiLU** is common in modern CNNs.

![GELU and SiLU both dip below zero before curving upward.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/gelu-silu.svg)

### 3.8 Softplus
```
softplus(z) = ln(1 + e^z)       smooth version of ReLU, always > 0
```
- Useful when an output must be **strictly positive**, e.g. a standard deviation σ in probabilistic forecasting.

![Softplus rounds the ReLU corner and stays above zero even for negative inputs.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/softplus-relu.svg)

### 3.9 Softmax (output layer, multi-class)
```
softmax(z_i) = e^(z_i) / Σ_j e^(z_j)
```
- Converts a vector of raw scores (**logits**) to probabilities that **sum to 1**.
- **Example:** scores `[2, 1, 0]` → e² = 7.389, e¹ = 2.718, e⁰ = 1 → sum = 11.107 → probabilities ≈ `[0.665, 0.245, 0.090]`.
- Adding the same number to all scores doesn't change the result, so implementations subtract the max for stability.
- **Temperature:** dividing scores by T > 1 flattens the probabilities; T < 1 sharpens them.

![Softmax turns scores 2, 1, and 0 into probabilities of approximately 66.5%, 24.5%, and 9.0%, preserving their ranking.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/softmax-scores.svg)

![The same logits produce sharper probabilities at low temperature and flatter probabilities at high temperature.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/temperature-bars.svg)

### 3.10 Linear (Identity)
- No activation. Used for **regression outputs** where any real number is allowed.

## 4. How to Choose

| Where | Task | Activation |
|---|---|---|
| Hidden layers (default) | MLP / CNN | **ReLU** |
| Hidden layers | Many dead neurons | Leaky ReLU / ELU |
| Hidden layers | Transformers | **GELU** (or SwiGLU variants) |
| Hidden layers | RNN/LSTM internals | tanh and sigmoid (already built in) |
| Output | Binary classification | **Sigmoid** |
| Output | Multi-class (one label) | **Softmax** |
| Output | Multi-label (several labels at once) | Sigmoid per label |
| Output | Regression (any value) | **Linear** |
| Output | Regression, must be strictly positive (e.g. σ) | **Softplus** |
| Output | Bounded value in (0, 1) | Sigmoid |

## 5. Gradients Through Activations

During backpropagation, the gradient is multiplied by the activation's **derivative** at each layer. So the derivative shapes how well learning signals travel back.

### 5.1 The Vanishing Gradient Problem
Sigmoid's derivative is at most 0.25. In a simplified calculation along one path, assuming weights of about 1 in magnitude, the activation derivatives multiply through many layers:

![From the output back through three layers, each gradient bar is one quarter the length of the previous bar.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Animated/gradient-shrinkage.svg)

```
5 layers:   0.25^5  ≈ 0.001
10 layers:  0.25^10 ≈ 0.000001   (about 1 in a million)
```
In this example, early layers receive almost no learning signal, so they barely learn. Actual gradients also depend on the weights and the combined contributions of different paths. Sigmoid and tanh networks historically struggled beyond a few layers for this reason.

### 5.2 The Exploding Gradient Problem
If each factor is larger than 1 (e.g. large weights), the product grows exponentially, so updates become huge and the loss becomes NaN. Common in RNNs.

![In a toy backward chain, doubling at each step grows a gradient from 1 to 16 in four steps.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/exploding-gradient.svg)

### 5.3 Remedies

| Problem | Fix |
|---|---|
| Vanishing | **ReLU-family** activations; proper **initialisation**; **batch/layer normalisation**; **residual (skip) connections**; LSTM/GRU for sequences |
| Exploding | **Gradient clipping**; smaller learning rate; good initialisation; normalisation |
| Dead ReLU | Leaky ReLU / ELU; lower learning rate; careful initialisation |

![Norm clipping shortens a gradient vector from magnitude five to magnitude two without changing its direction.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/gradient-clipping.svg)

### 5.4 Residual Connections (Skip Connections)
`output = layer(x) + x`. The "+ x" gives gradients a direct highway back, which is what made networks with hundreds of layers (ResNet) trainable.

![An animated residual block shows the input passing along two paths, with the original input added to the transformed result.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Animated/residual-path.svg)

## 6. Weight Initialisation

Starting weights should keep activations and gradients at a stable scale:
- **All zeros:** bad. Every neuron in a layer behaves identically (symmetry).
- **Too large / too small:** signals explode or shrink layer after layer.
- **Xavier/Glorot:** variance ≈ 2/(n_in + n_out). Suits **tanh/sigmoid**.
- **He:** variance ≈ 2/n_in. Suits **ReLU-family**.

Frameworks apply sensible defaults, but know which to pick when building custom layers.

![When two units start identically and receive identical updates, they stay identical. Different starting weights can break that symmetry.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/initialisation-symmetry.svg)

## 7. Code

### 7.1 NumPy
```python
import numpy as np

def sigmoid(z): return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))
def relu(z):    return np.maximum(0, z)
def leaky(z, a=0.01): return np.where(z > 0, z, a*z)
def softmax(z):
    e = np.exp(z - np.max(z))     # subtract max for numerical stability
    return e / e.sum()

z = np.array([-2, -1, 0, 1, 2])
print(sigmoid(z).round(3))        # [0.119 0.269 0.5   0.731 0.881]
print(relu(z))                    # [0 0 0 1 2]
print(softmax(np.array([2., 1., 0.])).round(3))   # [0.665 0.245 0.09 ]
```

### 7.2 PyTorch: a small deep network
```python
import torch.nn as nn

model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(20, 64), nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(64, 64), nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(64, 32), nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(32, 3)          # 3 raw scores (logits)
)
# For multi-class, use nn.CrossEntropyLoss(), which applies softmax internally.
```

## 8. Common Mistakes
- Using **sigmoid in all hidden layers** of a deep network.
- Applying **softmax before** a loss that already includes it.
- Putting an activation on a **regression output** that should be unbounded.
- Using **ReLU on an output that can be negative**.
- Initialising all weights to the same value.


## Reading note

ReLU is not differentiable at zero. Using a derivative of zero there is a common implementation convention, not a unique mathematical derivative.

entities.body:
# Chapter 5: Demand Forecasting and Time-Series Forecasting

**Level:** Beginner | **Reading time:** ~50 minutes

## Learning Objectives
## Contents

- [Learning Objectives](#learning-objectives)
- [1. What Is Time-Series Forecasting?](#1-what-is-time-series-forecasting)
- [2. Anatomy of a Time Series](#2-anatomy-of-a-time-series)
- [3. Key Statistical Ideas](#3-key-statistical-ideas)
- [4. Framing Forecasting as Supervised Learning](#4-framing-forecasting-as-supervised-learning)
- [5. Forecast Horizon and Multi-Step Strategies](#5-forecast-horizon-and-multi-step-strategies)
- [6. Models](#6-models)
- [7. An LSTM Forecaster in PyTorch](#7-an-lstm-forecaster-in-pytorch)
- [8. Preparing and Splitting Data Correctly](#8-preparing-and-splitting-data-correctly)
- [9. Evaluation Metrics](#9-evaluation-metrics)
- [10. Special Situations](#10-special-situations)
- [11. From Forecast to Decision](#11-from-forecast-to-decision)
- [12. Common Pitfalls](#12-common-pitfalls)
- [Key Takeaways](#key-takeaways)
- [Practice Questions](#practice-questions)
- [Answer Key](#answer-key)

- What a time series is, and what demand forecasting is for
- Trend, seasonality, stationarity, autocorrelation
- How to turn forecasting into a supervised learning problem
- Models from naive baselines to LSTMs and Transformers
- How to split data and validate correctly
- Metrics (MAE, RMSE, MAPE, WAPE, MASE, bias) and how to choose
- Special cases: intermittent demand, many products, hierarchies

---

## 1. What Is Time-Series Forecasting?

A **time series** is a sequence of observations ordered in time, usually at regular intervals (hourly, daily, weekly). **Forecasting** predicts future values from past values and known future information.

**Demand forecasting** predicts how much of a product or service customers will want. It drives decisions on:
- **Inventory:** how much to stock or order
- **Staffing:** how many people to schedule
- **Production and logistics:** what to make and ship
- **Pricing and promotion planning**

The cost of errors is usually **asymmetric**:
- Forecast too high → excess stock, waste, tied-up cash
- Forecast too low → lost sales, unhappy customers

(Chapter 6 shows how probabilistic forecasts handle this asymmetry.)

![Past observations end at a forecast cutoff, followed by future predictions and an uncertainty band.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/forecast-window.svg)

## 2. Anatomy of a Time Series

| Component | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Level** | The baseline average | ~200 units per day |
| **Trend** | Long-term rise or fall | Sales growing 10% a year |
| **Seasonality** | Repeating pattern at a fixed period | Weekend peaks; summer peaks; December spike |
| **Cycles** | Irregular longer waves | Business or economic cycles |
| **Calendar effects** | Holidays, paydays, events | Black Friday |
| **Noise** | Random variation | Unexplained daily jitter |

A series can combine them:
- **Additive:** `value = trend + seasonality + noise` (seasonal swings have constant size)
- **Multiplicative:** `value = trend × seasonality × noise` (swings grow with the level)

Multiplicative patterns can be made additive by taking the **logarithm**.

**Multiple seasonalities:** hourly electricity demand has daily, weekly and yearly cycles at once.

**External drivers (covariates / exogenous variables):** price, promotions, weather, holidays, competitor actions, marketing spend, stock availability.

![Toy signals isolate level, increasing trend, and a fixed-period seasonal cycle. The final signal combines trend and seasonality.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/ts-components.svg)

## 3. Key Statistical Ideas

### 3.1 Stationarity
A series is **stationary** if its statistical properties (mean, variance, autocorrelation) don't change over time. Classic models like ARIMA rely on it: the "I" (integrated) step differences the series until it is stationary. Make a series more stationary by:
- **Differencing:** `y_t − y_(t−1)` (removes trend), or `y_t − y_(t−7)` (removes weekly seasonality)
- **Log transform:** stabilises growing variance

Neural networks don't strictly require stationarity but still **train better on scaled, detrended or normalised inputs**.

![The increasing series 10,12,14,16,18 becomes four constant increments of two when adjacent values are subtracted.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/ts-differencing.svg)

### 3.2 Autocorrelation
How strongly a series correlates with its own **lagged** values. A strong correlation at lag 7 in daily data signals weekly seasonality. Plotting the **autocorrelation function (ACF)** helps you choose which lags to feed a model.

![This autocorrelation is calculated from six periods of a seven-day sinusoidal series. Peaks at lags seven and fourteen reflect weekly repetition. Finite-sample autocorrelation peaks decrease with lag.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/ts-seasonal-acf.svg)

## 4. Framing Forecasting as Supervised Learning

Neural networks need input/output pairs. Create them with a **sliding window**:

```
Series: 10, 12, 13, 15, 14, 16, 18      window = 3, horizon = 1

Input         → Target
[10, 12, 13]  → 15
[12, 13, 15]  → 14
[13, 15, 14]  → 16
[15, 14, 16]  → 18
```

```python
import numpy as np

def make_windows(series, window, horizon=1):
    X, y = [], []
    for i in range(len(series) - window - horizon + 1):
        X.append(series[i : i + window])
        y.append(series[i + window : i + window + horizon])
    return np.array(X), np.array(y)

X, y = make_windows(np.array([10, 12, 13, 15, 14, 16, 18]), window=3)
```

![The three-step input window moves over the exact sequence from the chapter. Each next value, in green, is the one-step target.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Animated/ts-sliding-window.svg)

### 4.1 Useful Features
- **Lag features:** value 1 day ago, 7 days ago, 365 days ago
- **Rolling statistics:** 7-day mean, 28-day standard deviation
- **Calendar features:** day of week, month, week of year, holiday flag (often encoded cyclically with sine and cosine)
- **Known future inputs:** planned promotions, prices, holidays
- **Static features:** product category, store location, size

### 4.2 Cyclical Encoding (for features like hour or month)
```python
hour_sin = np.sin(2*np.pi*hour/24)
hour_cos = np.cos(2*np.pi*hour/24)
```
This tells the network that hour 23 and hour 0 are close.

![The twenty-four hours are placed on a circle. Hours twenty-three and zero are neighbors on the circle, illustrating sine and cosine encoding.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/ts-cyclic-clock.svg)

## 5. Forecast Horizon and Multi-Step Strategies

- **One-step:** predict the next value.
- **Multi-step:** predict several steps ahead (e.g. the next 14 days).

| Strategy | How | Pros / Cons |
|---|---|---|
| **Recursive** | Predict one step, feed it back as input | Simple, but errors accumulate |
| **Direct** | Separate model (or output) per step | No error feedback, but more models |
| **Multi-output (seq2vec)** | One network outputs the whole horizon | Efficient, shares structure |
| **Seq2seq / encoder-decoder** | Encode history, decode future step by step | Flexible, handles future covariates |

![Recursive forecasting feeds a predicted value back into the model to predict the next value. Multi-output forecasting emits the whole horizon from one input window.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Animated/ts-multistep.svg)

## 6. Models

| Model | Idea | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Naive** | Forecast = last value | Baseline #1 |
| **Seasonal naive** | Forecast = value from the same point last season | Baseline #2. Surprisingly hard to beat |
| **Moving average** | Mean of recent values | Smooths noise |
| **Exponential smoothing (ETS, Holt-Winters)** | Weighted averages with level, trend, seasonality | Strong for single series |
| **ARIMA / SARIMA** | Auto-regression plus differencing plus moving average | Classic; differencing makes the series stationary |
| **Prophet-style additive models** | Trend + seasonality + holidays | Easy, interpretable |
| **Gradient boosting (LightGBM)** on lag features | Tree model on engineered features | A very strong baseline in competitions |
| **MLP** | Dense network on windowed inputs and covariates | Simple neural baseline |
| **RNN / LSTM / GRU** | Reads the sequence step by step | Learns temporal dependencies |
| **1D CNN / TCN** | Convolutions across time | Fast, parallel, long receptive field |
| **N-BEATS / N-HiTS** | Stacks of MLP blocks with trend and seasonality structure | Strong pure neural forecasters |
| **Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT)** | Attention plus covariate handling plus interpretability | Multi-horizon, many series |
| **DeepAR** | Autoregressive LSTM across many series, probabilistic | Chapter 6 |

> **Honest advice:** for a single short series, simple statistical methods are often as good or better than neural networks. Neural networks win when you have **many related series** (thousands of products or stores) and rich covariates. One **global model** trained across all series can share patterns, handle new products and use the covariates.

### 6.1 Global vs Local Models
- **Local:** one model per series. Flexible but data-hungry per series, and impractical for thousands of series.
- **Global:** one model for all series, with series identity as an input (often an embedding). Shares strength across series.

![Local forecasting gives each series its own model. A global model learns from several related series and receives series identity as an input.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/ts-global-local.svg)

## 7. An LSTM Forecaster in PyTorch

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class LSTMForecaster(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, n_features=1, hidden=64, horizon=7):
        super().__init__()
        self.lstm = nn.LSTM(n_features, hidden, num_layers=2,
                            batch_first=True, dropout=0.1)
        self.head = nn.Linear(hidden, horizon)

    def forward(self, x):                  # x: (batch, window, features)
        out, _ = self.lstm(x)
        return self.head(out[:, -1, :])    # use the last time step

model = LSTMForecaster()
loss_fn = nn.L1Loss()                      # MAE
opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
```

![Each recurrent step combines the current input with the previous hidden state.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Animated/rnn-state.svg)

**Scaling.** Compute the mean and standard deviation on the **training period only**, then apply them to validation and test data:
```python
mu, sd = train.mean(), train.std()
train_s, val_s = (train - mu)/sd, (val - mu)/sd
# remember to invert the scaling on predictions: pred * sd + mu
```

## 8. Preparing and Splitting Data Correctly

1. **Never shuffle across time.** Split chronologically:
   ```
   |-------- train --------|--- validation ---|--- test ---|
   past                                                 latest
   ```
2. **Fit scalers and encoders on training data only.**
3. **Avoid leakage:** don't use information unavailable at forecast time (e.g. next week's actual weather instead of the weather *forecast*; or a 7-day rolling mean that includes the target day).
4. **Handle missing data:** distinguish true zero sales from **stock-outs** (zero sales because there was nothing to sell). Stock-outs hide true demand.
5. **Handle outliers and special events:** flag them (promotions, outages) rather than silently deleting.
6. **Cold-start products:** use category, price and similar items.

![Earlier observations are used for training, followed by a validation period and a final test period. Fitting preprocessing uses the training portion only.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/ts-time-split.svg)

![On an illustrative stock-out day, observed sales stop at eight available units. Additional desired purchases are unobserved, so sales alone cannot reveal total demand.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/ts-stockout.svg)

### 8.1 Rolling-Origin (Walk-Forward) Validation
A single split can be misleading. Instead, repeatedly train on a growing past and test on the next block:

```
Fold 1: train [1..100]   test [101..114]
Fold 2: train [1..114]   test [115..128]
Fold 3: train [1..128]   test [129..142]
```
Average the errors. This mimics real deployment. In scikit-learn: `TimeSeriesSplit`.

![Three folds have expanding training histories and immediately following held-out blocks. Test blocks never precede their training history.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/ts-rolling-origin.svg)

## 9. Evaluation Metrics

Example: actual = `[100, 120, 90]`, forecast = `[110, 115, 100]`, errors (forecast − actual) = `[10, −5, 10]`, absolute errors = `[10, 5, 10]`.

| Metric | Formula | Result | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **MAE** | mean(\|e\|) | (10+5+10)/3 = **8.33** | Same units as data; robust |
| **MSE** | mean(e²) | (100+25+100)/3 = **75** | Penalises big errors |
| **RMSE** | √MSE | **8.66** | Same units; sensitive to outliers |
| **MAPE** | mean(\|e\|/\|actual\|)×100 | (10% + 4.17% + 11.11%)/3 ≈ **8.43%** | Breaks at actual = 0; favours under-forecasting |
| **WAPE** | Σ\|e\| / Σ\|actual\| | 25/310 = **8.06%** | Good for demand; handles zeros and mixed scales |
| **MASE** | MAE / MAE of the naive forecast (in-sample) | < 1 means beats naive | Scale-free; compare across series |
| **Bias** | mean(forecast − actual) | (10 − 5 + 10)/3 = **+5** | Positive = over-forecasting |

**Choosing:**
- Business-friendly percentage: **WAPE**
- Comparing across series with different scales: **MASE**
- Large errors are especially costly: **RMSE**
- Always report **bias** too. A forecast with low error but persistent bias still causes systematic over- or under-stocking.
- Always compare against the **seasonal naive baseline**.

![For actual values 100,120,90 and forecasts 110,115,100, the vertical gaps are plus ten, minus five, and plus ten units.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/ts-residuals.svg)

## 10. Special Situations

### 10.1 Intermittent (Lumpy) Demand
Spare parts or slow sellers have many zero-sales days. Standard models and MAPE fail. Use **Croston's method** (models demand size and interval separately), count distributions (Poisson, negative binomial), or probabilistic neural models (Chapter 6).

![Twelve illustrative days contain nine zero-demand days and three nonzero days. Separate gaps and nonzero sizes help explain intermittent demand.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/ts-intermittent.svg)

### 10.2 Hierarchies
Sales roll up: SKU → category → store → region → total. Forecasts at different levels should **add up consistently**. Use **hierarchical reconciliation** (e.g. top-down, bottom-up, MinT).

![SKU forecasts of ten and twenty sum to category thirty. A second category of forty makes a total of seventy.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/ts-hierarchy.svg)

### 10.3 New Products (Cold Start)
No history. Use attributes (category, price, brand) and "similar product" histories, or global models with embeddings.

### 10.4 Promotions and Price Effects
Include price, discount depth and promo flags as covariates, and consider **cannibalisation** (a promotion on one item reduces others).

### 10.5 Forecast Value Added (FVA)
Measure whether each step (statistical model, neural network, human adjustment) actually improves on the previous one. Many manual overrides make forecasts worse.

## 11. From Forecast to Decision

A forecast only matters through the decision it drives. Example, a simple **safety stock** idea:
```
order quantity = forecast demand over lead time + safety stock
```
The safety stock depends on the forecast's **uncertainty** and the target service level, which motivates probabilistic forecasting (Chapter 6).

![A simplified order quantity consists of forecast demand over lead time plus safety stock. The illustration assigns forecast demand one hundred and safety stock twenty.](/materials/Assets/Connectionist%20AI/Static/ts-inventory-decision.svg)

## 12. Common Pitfalls
- Random train/test split (the model "sees the future")
- Scaling using the entire dataset (leakage)
- No baseline comparison
- Ignoring holidays, promotions, stock-outs
- Optimising MAPE and ending up with systematically low forecasts
- Forgetting that patterns change (concept drift, Chapter 7)
- Using a deep model when a seasonal naive nearly matches it

## Key Takeaways
- Break a series into level, trend, seasonality, calendar effects and noise.
- Turn forecasting into supervised learning with windows, lags and covariates.
- Split by time, use walk-forward validation, avoid leakage.
- Always beat a seasonal naive baseline, and report bias along with error.
- Neural networks shine with many related series and rich covariates.

---

## Practice Questions

1. Name the trend, seasonality and noise in: "Sales rise slowly each year, jump every December, and vary randomly day to day."
2. Window size 2 on `[5, 7, 6, 8, 9]`: list the input → target pairs.
3. Why not shuffle a time series before splitting?
4. MAE for actual `[50, 60]`, forecast `[55, 54]`?
5. What is a seasonal naive forecast?
6. Why encode hour of day with sine and cosine?
7. WAPE if total absolute error is 30 and total actual demand is 400?
8. What is a stock-out, and why does it distort demand data?
9. When might ARIMA beat an LSTM?
10. Recursive vs direct multi-step forecasting?

---

## Answer Key

1. Trend: slow yearly rise. Seasonality: December jump. Noise: daily randomness.
2. `[5,7]→6`, `[7,6]→8`, `[6,8]→9`.
3. It leaks future data into training and inflates results.
4. (5 + 6)/2 = **5.5**.
5. Use the value from the same point in the previous season (e.g. same weekday last week).
6. So hour 23 and hour 0 are recognised as close neighbours.
7. 30/400 = **7.5%**.
8. Zero sales because nothing was available, so recorded sales understate true demand.
9. A single short series with little data.
10. Recursive feeds predictions back as inputs (errors accumulate); direct uses a separate model/output per step.


## Reading note

A target stock level is not an order quantity. An order must also account for inventory on hand, outstanding orders and backorders.
