entities.title: Test bank A22
entities.prompt: A recursive function can work correctly without a base case, as long as the input is small.
entities.explanation: Without a base case the function never stops calling itself, whatever the input; the call stack grows until the program fails (in Python, a RecursionError). Every recursive function needs a base case.

entities.title: Test bank A23
entities.prompt: A deque (double-ended queue) allows items to be added and removed at both ends.
entities.explanation: That is what "double-ended" means. Input-restricted and output-restricted deques limit one of the two operations to one end.

entities.title: Test bank A24
entities.prompt: In a binary search tree, every value in a node's left subtree is smaller than that node's value.
entities.explanation: That is the BST rule: left subtree smaller, right subtree larger. It lets a search go left or right at each node.

entities.title: Test bank A25
entities.prompt: In an undirected graph, an edge can only be followed in one direction.
entities.explanation: Undirected edges work both ways, like a friendship: if Nicky is linked to Neil, Neil is linked to Nicky. Edges with one direction belong to a directed graph.

entities.title: Test bank A26
entities.prompt: Inserting the keys 1, 3, 8, 10 into an empty binary search tree in that order produces a balanced tree.
entities.explanation: Each new key is larger than all the others, so each becomes a right child: the tree is a chain of height 4, and searching it is as slow as a linked list (O(n)).

entities.title: Test bank A27
entities.prompt: In a binary search tree, the successor of a key is the next larger key in sorted order.
entities.explanation: If the node has a right subtree, the successor is the smallest key there; otherwise it is the first ancestor reached from a left child.

entities.title: Test bank A28
entities.prompt: In an artificial neuron, the bias is multiplied by one of the inputs before it is added.
entities.explanation: Each input is multiplied by its weight; the bias is then added on its own. It shifts the result, like the b in y = mx + b.

entities.title: Test bank A29
entities.prompt: A single neuron that draws one straight line can learn XOR.
entities.explanation: XOR's two 1s are on opposite corners, (0, 1) and (1, 0), and no single straight line separates them from (0, 0) and (1, 1). A hidden layer is needed.

entities.title: Test bank A30
entities.prompt: A dense layer with 3 inputs and 4 neurons has 16 parameters.
entities.explanation: 3 × 4 = 12 weights plus 4 biases = 16.

entities.title: Test bank A31
entities.prompt: Stacking many layers without non-linear activation functions still gives a network that can only learn linear (straight-line) relationships.
entities.explanation: Each layer computes Wx + b, and two such layers combine into one: W₂(W₁x + b₁) + b₂ = (W₂W₁)x + (W₂b₁ + b₂). Any number of them is still one linear function.

entities.title: Test bank A32
entities.prompt: A defect detector that is 98% accurate on bottles of which 2% are defective must be good at finding defects.
entities.explanation: A model that always answers "ok" is 98% accurate on this data and finds no defects at all. For rare events, check recall: the share of real defects that are found.

entities.title: Test bank A33
entities.prompt: Before testing a forecasting model, the time series should be shuffled randomly and then split into training and test sets.
entities.explanation: Time series must be split by time: train on the past and test on the future. Shuffling lets the model learn from days that come after the test days, so the results look better than real use.

entities.title: Test bank A34
entities.prompt: Actual demand should be at or below a well-calibrated P90 forecast about 90% of the time.
entities.explanation: That is the meaning of the 90% quantile. If demand is below it much less often, the forecast is too low; much more often, too high.

entities.title: Test bank A35
entities.prompt: A positive forecast bias means the forecasts are, on average, too low.
entities.explanation: Bias = average of (forecast − actual). A positive bias means the forecasts are too high on average; a negative bias means too low.

entities.title: Test bank A36
entities.prompt: In online learning, the model is updated after each new example arrives.
entities.explanation: Online learning updates after every single example and then discards it. Batch learning trains on all the data at once.

entities.title: Test bank A37
entities.prompt: Collaborative filtering needs a description of each item's content, such as its genre, to make recommendations.
entities.explanation: Collaborative filtering uses only the pattern of ratings or clicks across users. Content-based filtering is the method that uses item features.

entities.title: Test bank A38
entities.prompt: In reinforcement learning, the agent is told the correct action for each state.
entities.explanation: The agent only receives rewards, often only at the end. It must discover good actions by trial and error. Being told the correct answer is supervised learning.

entities.title: Test bank A39
entities.prompt: With a discount factor of γ = 0, the agent cares only about the immediate reward.
entities.explanation: Later rewards are multiplied by γ, γ², …, which are all 0. A γ close to 1 makes the agent far-sighted.

entities.title: Test bank A40
entities.prompt: A training loss far lower than the validation loss is a sign of overfitting.
entities.explanation: The model fits the training data much better than new data, so it has memorised details instead of learning the general pattern.

entities.title: Test bank B1
entities.prompt: Which of the following is not a required property of an algorithm?
options: Its steps are precise and unambiguous.
It finishes after a finite number of steps.
entities.explanation: An algorithm can be written in any form (steps, pseudocode, flowchart) or any language. A, B and D are required properties: output, definiteness and finiteness.

entities.title: Test bank B2
entities.prompt: In a flowchart, which shape is used for a yes/no decision such as "Is score > highest?"
entities.explanation: Diamond = decision. Oval = start/end, rectangle = process step, parallelogram = input/output.

entities.title: Test bank B3
entities.prompt: Bubble sort (ascending) is applied to [5, 1, 4]. What is the list after the first pass?
entities.explanation: 5 > 1, swap → [1, 5, 4]; 5 > 4, swap → [1, 4, 5]. Option A is the list after only the first comparison.

entities.title: Test bank B4
entities.prompt: How many comparisons does bubble sort with early exit make on the already-sorted list [29, 40, 72, 85, 91, 100]?
entities.explanation: One pass compares the 5 neighbouring pairs, makes no swaps, and stops. Without the early-exit check it would always make all 5 passes: 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15 comparisons, even on a sorted list.

entities.title: Test bank B5
entities.prompt: Selection sort (ascending) is applied to [4, 3, 1, 2]. What is the list after the first pass?
entities.explanation: Pass 1 finds the smallest value, 1, and swaps it with the first card, 4: [1, 3, 4, 2]. Option B is one pass of bubble sort, option C is the fully sorted list, and option D shifts the others instead of swapping.

entities.title: Test bank B6
entities.prompt: Insertion sort is working on [40, 72, 85, 29]. The first three cards are already in order. How many comparisons does it make to insert 29?
entities.explanation: 29 is compared with 85, 72 and 40. Each is bigger, so each shifts right and 29 reaches the front: 3 comparisons, 3 shifts.

entities.title: Test bank B7
entities.prompt: Binary search looks for 14 in [2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16], always checking the lower middle when there is an even number of items. Which values does it check, in order?
entities.explanation: Middle of 8 items = 8 (14 is larger, keep 10–16); middle = 12 (keep 14–16); middle = 14, found. Option A is linear search.

entities.title: Test bank B8
entities.prompt: A sorted list has 1,024 items. How many times can binary search halve the range before only one item is left?

entities.title: Test bank B9
entities.prompt: Which growth rate means the most work for very large n?
entities.explanation: For large n: 1 < log n < n < n². For n = 1,000,000, n² is a trillion.

entities.title: Test bank B10
entities.prompt: Which operation takes O(n) time in the worst case?
options: Reading an array item by its index
Linear search in an unsorted list
Dequeuing the front item of a queue
entities.explanation: Linear search may check all n items. The other three are O(1) operations.

entities.title: Test bank B11
entities.prompt: During BFS on the B.O.T.A.K. maze, what does the number written in each cell mean?
options: The order in which DFS visited it
The number of walls next to it
Its number of steps from S along a shortest route
entities.explanation: BFS numbers each cell with its distance from S, wave by wave. That is why G's number (7) is the length of the shortest route.

entities.title: Test bank B12
entities.prompt: A tree has root A; A's children are B and C; B's children are D and E; C's child is F. Visiting left neighbours first, which is a BFS order from A?
options: A, B, D, E, C, F
A, B, C, D, E, F
A, C, F, B, E, D
D, E, B, F, C, A
entities.explanation: BFS goes level by level: A (distance 0), B and C (distance 1), then D, E, F (distance 2). Option A is the DFS order.

entities.title: Test bank B13
entities.prompt: A tree has root A; A's children are B and C; B's children are D and E; C's child is F. Using this tree and visiting left neighbours first, which is a DFS order from A?
options: A, B, C, D, E, F
A, C, B, F, E, D
F, E, D, C, B, A
A, B, D, E, C, F
entities.explanation: DFS goes as deep as possible first: A → B → D, back to B → E, back to A → C → F.

entities.title: Test bank B14
entities.prompt: Dijkstra's algorithm runs on a graph with edges S–A (1), A–G (8), S–B (2), B–C (2) and C–G (2). What is the cheapest cost from S to G?
entities.explanation: Settle S (0) → A = 1, B = 2; settle A → G = 9; settle B → C = 4; settle C → G = min(9, 6) = 6. The route is S → B → C → G. Option A (9) is the fewest-edges route S → A → G that BFS would choose.

entities.title: Test bank B15
entities.prompt: Coins come in 1, 3 and 4. Botak-Bot gives 6 in change using the greedy rule "take the biggest coin that still fits". How many coins does it use, and is that the fewest possible?
options: 2 coins; yes, it is the fewest
3 coins; yes, it is the fewest
entities.explanation: Greedy takes 4, then 1, then 1: 3 coins. But 3 + 3 = 6 uses only 2 coins, so the greedy choice of 4 was not part of the best answer.

entities.title: Test bank B16
entities.prompt: A program reads items by their position very often and almost never inserts items in the middle. Which structure fits best?
entities.explanation: Arrays give O(1) access by index. Linked lists need O(n) to reach a position, and stacks and queues only give access at their ends.

entities.title: Test bank B17
entities.prompt: Which statement about a singly linked list is correct?
options: Each node stores a value and a link to the next node.
Its nodes must be stored next to each other in memory.
Reaching the k-th node takes O(1) time.
It cannot grow after it is created.
entities.explanation: That is the definition of a node. Nodes can be anywhere in memory (B false), reaching the k-th node takes O(n) (C false), and lists grow easily by adding nodes (D false).

entities.title: Test bank B18
entities.prompt: The array [72, 85, 91] has room for one more item. What is the array after inserting 80 at index 1?
entities.explanation: Index 1 is the second position. 85 and 91 each shift one place right to make room, keeping their order.

entities.title: Test bank B19
entities.prompt: Start with an empty stack. Do: push A, push B, pop, push C, push D, pop. Which item is on top now?
entities.explanation: [A] → [A, B] → pop B → [A] → [A, C] → [A, C, D] → pop D → [A, C]. The top is C.

entities.title: Test bank B20
entities.prompt: Start with an empty queue. Do: enqueue Ana, enqueue Ben, enqueue Cai, dequeue, enqueue Dee, dequeue. Who is at the front now?
entities.explanation: Ana, Ben, Cai → Ana leaves → Ben, Cai, Dee → Ben leaves → Cai, Dee. Cai is at the front.

entities.title: Test bank B21
entities.prompt: Select all that apply. Which are typical uses of a stack?
options: Serving print jobs in the order they arrive
entities.explanation: Undo, bracket matching and function calls all need the most recent item first (LIFO). Print jobs in arrival order need a queue (FIFO).

entities.title: Test bank B22
entities.prompt: factorial(n) returns 1 when n == 1, and otherwise returns n × factorial(n − 1). When factorial(3) runs, which call finishes (returns) first?
options: They all finish at the same time
entities.explanation: factorial(3) waits for factorial(2), which waits for factorial(1). The base case factorial(1) is the last call pushed onto the call stack and the first to return (LIFO); then factorial(2) returns 2, then factorial(3) returns 6.

entities.title: Test bank B23
entities.prompt: Which describes an input-restricted deque?
options: Items are added at one end only, but can be removed from both ends.
Items can be added at both ends, but are removed from one end only.
Items are removed in order of priority.
Items can only be added when the deque is empty.
entities.explanation: Input (adding) is restricted to one end; removing is allowed at both ends. Option B describes an output-restricted deque, and option C a priority queue.

entities.title: Test bank B24
entities.prompt: In a friendship network, Nicky is linked to Darren and Neil, Neil is linked to Glen, and Darren is linked to Glen. Using BFS from Nicky, how many edges are on the shortest route to Glen?
entities.explanation: Distance 1: Darren and Neil. Distance 2: Glen (Nicky → Neil → Glen or Nicky → Darren → Glen). Nicky and Glen are not linked directly, so 1 is wrong.

entities.title: Test bank B25
entities.prompt: A binary search tree has root 8, left child 3 (whose left child is 1) and right child 10. Where is 5 inserted?
entities.explanation: 5 < 8, go left to 3; 5 > 3, go right; that spot is empty, so 5 becomes the right child of 3.

entities.title: Test bank B26
entities.prompt: A BST has root 8 with children 3 and 10; 3 has left child 1 and right child 6, and 6 has right child 7. If 3 is deleted using its successor, which key takes its place?
entities.explanation: 3 has two children, so it is replaced by its successor, the smallest key in its right subtree: 6. Then 7 moves up into the old place of 6. Inorder afterwards: 1, 6, 7, 8, 10.

entities.title: Test bank B27
entities.prompt: In the adjacency matrix of the friendship network (Nicky–Darren, Nicky–Neil, Darren–Glen, Neil–Glen), what is in the cell for row Nicky, column Glen?
entities.explanation: 0, because there is no edge between Nicky and Glen. They are two edges apart, but a matrix cell only records a direct edge. Option D is what an adjacency list stores for Nicky.

entities.title: Test bank B28
entities.prompt: A ReLU neuron has inputs [1, 3], weights [0.5, −0.5] and bias 0.2. What is its output?
entities.explanation: z = 0.5 × 1 − 0.5 × 3 + 0.2 = −0.8. ReLU turns negative values into 0, so the output is 0. Option B forgets the activation.

entities.title: Test bank B29
entities.prompt: How many parameters (weights and biases) does a dense layer with 4 inputs and 2 neurons have?
entities.explanation: 4 × 2 = 8 weights plus 2 biases = 10. Option A forgets the biases.

entities.title: Test bank B30
entities.prompt: A weight is 0.5, its gradient is 2 and the learning rate is 0.1. What is the weight after one gradient-descent step?
entities.explanation: new w = w − learning rate × gradient = 0.5 − 0.1 × 2 = 0.3. A positive gradient means increasing w would raise the loss, so w goes down. Option A moves in the wrong direction.

entities.title: Test bank B31
entities.prompt: A network must decide which of 10 digits (0–9) is in an image. Which output activation fits best?
entities.explanation: Softmax turns the 10 scores into probabilities that add up to 1, for choosing one class out of many. Sigmoid suits one yes/no output, linear suits any number, and softplus suits a number that must be above 0.

entities.title: Test bank B32
entities.prompt: Why is ReLU usually preferred to sigmoid in the hidden layers of a deep network?
options: ReLU always outputs values between 0 and 1.
ReLU makes the network linear, which is easier to train.
ReLU's slope is 1 for positive inputs, so the learning signal shrinks less across many layers.
entities.explanation: Sigmoid's slope is at most 0.25, so multiplying it across many layers makes the gradient vanish. ReLU is not bounded above (A false), is non-linear (B false), and outputs 0 for negative inputs (D false).

entities.title: Test bank B33
entities.prompt: Select all that apply. Which situations suit a neural network well?
options: Recognising objects in thousands of labelled photos
Adding up a short list of prices exactly
Predicting from 10 rows of data when every decision must be fully explained
entities.explanation: Neural networks shine with lots of data and messy inputs such as images and audio. Exact arithmetic needs a simple rule, and a tiny dataset that must be fully explained suits a simpler model.

entities.title: Test bank B34
entities.prompt: Actual sales are [10, 20, 30] and the forecasts are [12, 18, 33]. What is the mean absolute error (MAE)?
entities.explanation: The errors (forecast − actual) are +2, −2 and +3; their absolute values add up to 7, and 7 / 3 ≈ 2.33. Option A is the bias (average signed error), and option B is the total before dividing.

entities.title: Test bank B35
entities.prompt: Running out of a cake loses 4 in profit, and each leftover cake wastes 1. Using the newsvendor rule, which quantile of the demand forecast should the shop stock to?
entities.explanation: Stock to shortage cost ÷ (shortage cost + leftover cost) = 4 / (4 + 1) = 0.8, the P80. Running out costs four times more than a leftover, so it pays to stock above the median (P50).

entities.title: Test bank B36
entities.prompt: A P90 (τ = 0.9) forecast is 110 and the actual value is 100. What is the pinball loss?
entities.explanation: The forecast is too high by 10, so the loss is (1 − 0.9) × 10 = 1. If it had been too low by 10, the loss would be 0.9 × 10 = 9 (option A).

entities.title: Test bank B37
entities.prompt: The mean of 5 values is 6. A sixth value, 12, arrives. What is the new mean, updated without storing the old values?
entities.explanation: new mean = old mean + (new value − old mean) / n = 6 + (12 − 6) / 6 = 7. Check: (5 × 6 + 12) / 6 = 42 / 6 = 7. Option A averages only the old mean and the new value.

entities.title: Test bank B38
entities.prompt: A recommender shows 5 films. 2 of them are relevant to the user, who has 4 relevant films in total. What are Precision@5 and Recall@5?
entities.explanation: Precision@5 = relevant shown / shown = 2 / 5 = 0.4. Recall@5 = relevant shown / all relevant = 2 / 4 = 0.5. Option A swaps them.

entities.title: Test bank B39
entities.prompt: Two users rate three films: A = [3, 4, 0] and B = [4, 3, 0]. What is their cosine similarity?
entities.explanation: A · B = 12 + 12 + 0 = 24; |A| = |B| = √25 = 5; 24 / (5 × 5) = 0.96. Their tastes are very similar but not identical, so the answer is close to but below 1.

entities.title: Test bank B40
entities.prompt: Q-learning: Q(s, a) = 0.5, α = 0.2, γ = 0.9, reward r = 1, and the best Q-value in the next state is 1. What is the new Q(s, a)?
entities.explanation: target = r + γ × max Q(s′, a′) = 1 + 0.9 × 1 = 1.9. new Q = 0.5 + 0.2 × (1.9 − 0.5) = 0.5 + 0.28 = 0.78. Option A is the target itself, which the update only moves part of the way towards.

entities.title: Test bank B41
entities.prompt: An agent uses the ε-greedy rule with ε = 0.1. What does it do?
options: It always takes the action with the highest Q-value.
It takes a random action about 90% of the time.
It stops training when its reward falls below 0.1.
It takes a random action about 10% of the time and the best-known action otherwise.
entities.explanation: With probability ε = 0.1 it explores (acts randomly); otherwise it exploits the best-known action. Option A would never explore, and option B swaps exploring and exploiting.

entities.title: Test bank B42
entities.prompt: After training, the training loss and the validation loss are both high and close together. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: The test set was used for tuning
entities.explanation: High error on both sets means the model has not learned the pattern: it is underfitting. Try a bigger model, train longer or improve the features. Overfitting shows low training error but high validation error.
